payload.name: Aggregate Count Memories for Owned Items
payload.description: When a user mentions multiple named pets or other countable owned items across a session, during extraction create an aggregate count memory; during CRUD update it when items are added or removed.
content: During extraction, if a user mentions multiple named pets or other countable owned items that belong to them and the messages establish the complete current set, create one compact profile memory stating the total count and the names (e.g., 'has 3 dogs: X, Y, Z') in addition to the individual pet/item memories.

Count only items explicitly owned by the speaker; exclude pets/items belonging to others and generic mentions with no owner. Create the aggregate only when the conversation/session makes the full current set clear; otherwise do not guess or search for more items.

During CRUD, when an aggregate count memory already exists, update it when a new same-category item is added or an existing item is removed, keeping names and count consistent; do not create a duplicate aggregate memory.
Stop after capturing the aggregate count for the stated category; do not add counts for other categories, infer unmentioned totals, or expand into extra searches.

candidates.solves: The construction pipeline records individual named pets or possessions but never saves the total count, so later questions like 'how many X does the user have?' cannot be answered from memory. This skill creates and maintains a compact aggregate count memory when multiple same-category owned items are mentioned.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Uses of Tools and Systems
payload.description: Use when a user states what they use an object, tool, system, or method for, listing explicit purposes.
content: During extraction, when a user mentions an item, tool, system, or method and explicitly lists what they use it for, capture each stated purpose as part of a candidate memory, even if the message also expresses motivation or emotion.
Preserve the concrete functions verbatim or near-verbatim; do not replace them with a general emotional or motivational summary.
If the same message contains distinct purposes, keep them together in one candidate for that item, unless they belong to separate memory kinds (e.g., event vs state) that should be split.

candidates.solves: When a user explicitly describes the purposes or functions of an object, tool, system, or method they use, extracted memories often collapse these concrete details into a vague emotional or motivational state, losing the specific uses. This skill ensures each stated use is preserved so future questions about what something is used for can be answered.

payload.name: Preserve Explicit Descriptions of Possessions and Pets
payload.description: When a user introduces or references a possession, pet, or item and explicitly describes it with adjectives, during extraction.
content: During extraction, if a user gives an explicit descriptive quality of a possession, pet, or item (e.g., 'super cozy and comfy', 'really reliable', 'beautiful'), create a state or preference memory linking that item to the exact description.
Do this even when the statement appears in a photo-sharing phrase or as a follow-up to an earlier mention; do not skip because the item was already known.
Record only adjectives or qualities explicitly stated; do not infer additional attributes, and stop after capturing the description.

candidates.solves: Prevents omission of users' explicit qualitative descriptions of their possessions, pets, or items, especially when those descriptions appear in photo-sharing or casual follow-up messages rather than in a dedicated statement.

payload.name: Preserve Enumerated Items in Recommendations
payload.description: When a speaker recommends, offers, or lists concrete items (supplies, tools, ingredients, materials), extract each named item rather than summarizing them as a category.
content: During extraction, if a message explicitly names multiple concrete items (e.g., acrylic paints, brushes, canvas/paper, palette) as recommended, offered, or needed, create the candidate content listing those exact items; do not replace the list with a generic label such as 'supplies' or 'gear'.
During CRUD, when merging or updating a memory that contains an itemized list, preserve every listed item; do not collapse specific items into a broader category unless new evidence contradicts them.
Capture only items explicitly stated in the message; stop after the stated list and do not infer additional materials.

candidates.solves: Extracted memories often paraphrase explicit enumerations (recommended supplies, ingredients, tools, or materials) into vague categories like 'supplies', losing specific facts that later questions need. This skill preserves each explicitly named item so future questions about the list can be answered from memory.

payload.name: Preserve Specific Object Names in Memory Extraction
payload.description: When a speaker names a specific object, device, or tool (e.g., fitness tracker, journal, app) that plays a role in their life, preserve that exact term in the memory instead of generalizing it.
content: During extraction, when a speaker refers to a specific object, device, or tool with a concrete name or phrase, record that exact term in the candidate memory content; do not replace it with a broader category such as 'tool' or 'device' unless the speaker themselves used that generic wording.
Apply this when the object is described as serving a role for the speaker, such as a reminder, motivation, tracking, or routine; preserve both the exact object term and the role it plays.
Stop after capturing the named object and its stated role; do not infer additional attributes, brands, or unmentioned capabilities.

candidates.solves: Prevents loss of specific facts when extraction paraphrases a user's named object into a generic category (e.g., 'fitness tracker' becomes 'tracking tool'), which can make memories only partially match later claims. It instructs the extraction stage to keep the user's exact term whenever a named object is given a role in the user's life.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Possession and Replacement Facts
payload.description: When a user states they have, got, bought, or replaced an item (e.g., car, house, gadget), during extraction.
content: During extraction, treat any explicit statement of ownership, acquisition, or replacement of a possession as a candidate memory, even if it appears in casual greetings or as background. Example: 'my new Prius' → the user's current car is a new Prius; 'I got a new phone' → the user has a new phone.

Record the item type and any stated descriptor (e.g., new, old, model name, color) in a profile or state memory. If the user mentions a previous item and its replacement, also create an event memory capturing the change.
Do not infer unstated reasons, upgrades, or additional possessions; capture only what is explicitly stated.
Stop after capturing the stated possession and any stated replacement; do not expand into related product preferences or comparisons.

candidates.solves: The construction agent sometimes fails to extract explicit statements about a user's possessions or acquisitions, especially when they are mentioned in casual greetings or as background ('my new Prius', 'I got a new phone'). As a result, future questions about what the user owns or what replaced an old item cannot be answered. This skill ensures that stated ownership, acquisition, or replacement facts are captured as durable memories.

payload.name: Extract Purchase Events from Photo-Sharing Messages
payload.description: When a message shares a photo and states in first person that the speaker bought, purchased, acquired, or obtained the depicted item, during extraction.
content: During extraction, when a message uses presentation phrasing such as 'Here are...' or 'This is a photo of...' and contains a first-person statement that the speaker bought, purchased, acquired, or otherwise obtained the depicted object, create an event candidate for that acquisition with actor, action, object, and time.

Resolve relative time expressions like 'the day before yesterday' or 'last week' using the message's occurred_at timestamp; do not skip the candidate because the time is relative or the fact is embedded in a photo-sharing turn.
Keep the acquisition event separate from any photo-sharing event; do not replace the acquisition with the act of sharing a photo.
Do not create acquisition candidates unless the speaker explicitly states the acquisition; do not infer ownership from merely showing a photo.

candidates.solves: Messages that share photos often contain embedded first-person statements about purchases or acquisitions of the depicted item. Without explicit guidance, the extraction stage may skip the turn or only capture the photo-sharing act, losing the durable event and its time. This skill ensures such embedded acquisition facts become event candidates with resolved dates.

payload.name: Extract Stated Decision Reasons
payload.description: During extraction, when a user states why they chose, decided, or got something (often in response to 'why did you decide...'), create a memory capturing the choice and its stated reason.
content: During extraction, when a user explicitly states the reason for a past decision they made (such as choosing a pet, hobby, job, or purchase), create a candidate preference or state memory capturing the decision and the reason in the user's own words.
Do not infer motivations the user does not state; record only the rationale explicitly given.

If the same statement also describes the item as providing comfort or joy, create a separate comfort-source memory (per existing skill) and keep the decision reason as its own candidate rather than merging.
Create at most one decision-reason memory per distinct decision; stop after capturing the stated reason.

candidates.solves: When a user gives the reason behind a personal decision (e.g., choosing a pet, hobby, job, or purchase), the construction pipeline sometimes fails to extract it, leaving the decision rationale absent from memory and later answerable questions unsupported.

payload.name: Preserve Exhibition Context for Created Works
payload.description: When a speaker mentions a work (painting, book, etc.) that is finished, published, or exhibited, during extraction include the publication/exhibition detail in the memory.
content: During extraction, if a speaker describes finishing or creating a work (e.g., painting, book, song) and also states that it is published, exhibited, or displayed, capture that contextual detail in the same event memory or as a related event/relationship memory.
Do not create a candidate that only records the creation action; preserve all explicitly stated identifiers that would let a future question identify the specific work.
During CRUD, when adding or updating memories about a created work, do not merge away an existing publication/exhibition detail unless new evidence directly contradicts it.
Stop after capturing the explicitly stated context; do not infer additional locations or publication details.

candidates.solves: When extraction summarizes an event about a created work, it can drop the contextual detail that identifies the work (e.g., that it was exhibited or published), making the memory insufficient for later questions that refer to that work by its context. This Skill ensures such explicit identifiers are preserved.

payload.name: Preserve Distinct Occurrence Events During SKIP Decisions
payload.description: When a message contains a distinct occurrence (received/sent/got X) alongside related feelings or impact, during CRUD do not skip the occurrence as already represented by a profile/preference memory.
content: During extraction, when a message states a distinct occurrence (e.g., receiving or sending correspondence, a gift, an award, or attending an event) alongside related attitudes or impact, emit that occurrence as its own event candidate.

During CRUD decisions, compare an event candidate only against existing event memories covering the same occurrence, sender/recipient, and time; do not SKIP it because a profile/preference memory was updated with related sentiments or impact.
If the same message also enriched a profile/preference memory, preserve both memories: the enrichment reflects durable traits and the event reflects the countable occurrence.
Stop once the distinct occurrence is stored; do not add inferred details about other letters, awards, or events.

candidates.solves: Memory construction can miss individual occurrences because a new event candidate is skipped as already represented when only a related profile/preference memory was updated. This skill ensures distinct events (e.g., receiving a letter, gift, or award) are preserved as separate event memories so future count and object questions can be answered.

payload.name: Preserve Explicitly Stated Reactions
payload.description: When a message explicitly describes how a person or pet reacted to a situation (e.g., confused, scared, excited), during extraction.
content: During extraction, if the speaker explicitly states a reaction or emotional/cognitive response of a person or pet to a situation (e.g., 'so confused', 'scared', 'excited'), preserve that exact stated reaction in the candidate memory content.
Do not replace the stated reaction with a broader inferred preference or general attitude; include both the triggering context and the explicit reaction.
Capture the reaction as part of the relevant preference/state/event memory, and during CRUD update an existing memory if it omits the explicitly stated reaction.
Do not add unstated reactions; stop after preserving what was explicitly said.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes summarizes an explicitly stated reaction (e.g., 'so confused') into a broader preference or attitude (e.g., 'dislikes snow'), losing the exact observable response. This makes memory unable to answer questions about how a person or pet reacted. The skill preserves explicitly stated reactions in candidate memories.

payload.name: Extract Recipients of Directly Announced Events
payload.description: When a message directly addresses a named person and announces a personal event or news, include the addressee as the recipient in the event memory.
content: During extraction, if the speaker directly addresses a named person (e.g., 'Hey Sam!') and shares a life event or news in the same message, create an event candidate that records both the event and that the speaker told/announced it to that addressee.
If the addressee is not named but is clearly the conversation partner being informed (e.g., the other participant in the session), record that person as the recipient of the news.
Do not infer additional recipients beyond the directly addressed or clearly informed person; stop after capturing the event and its recipient.

candidates.solves: When a speaker directly tells a named person about a personal event or news, extraction often records only the event and drops the recipient, making later 'who did X tell?' questions unanswerable. This skill ensures the addressee of a direct announcement is preserved in the memory.

payload.name: Extract Explicitly Named Media Titles with Engagement
payload.description: When a message names a specific game, movie, show, book, or other media title and states the user is playing, watching, or reading it, create a durable memory for that title even if the message contains other topics.
content: During extraction, if a message explicitly names a game, movie, TV show, book, or other media title and states the user is playing, watching, reading, or otherwise engaged with it, create a separate durable preference or event memory for that title with subject=user and world_start set to the message date.
Create one candidate per explicitly named media title; do not merge the title only into a general hobby, relationship, or other-topic candidate.

Include any intensity or temporal detail the user stated (e.g., 'nonstop', 'recently') when it is part of the claim, and stop once all explicitly named media titles in the message are captured—do not infer unmentioned titles.

candidates.solves: During candidate extraction, when a user names a specific game, movie, show, book, or other media title and describes playing, watching, or reading it, the construction agent sometimes skips creating a memory for that title when the same message also contains other extractable facts. This skill ensures each explicitly named media title with engagement is captured as its own durable memory.

payload.name: Preserve Explicit Creative Process Descriptions
payload.description: When a user explicitly describes the process, style, mood, or intent behind creating a work (e.g., painting, writing, project), preserve the specific phrasing in the memory.
content: When creating or updating a memory about a creative work, if the user explicitly states how they created it (process, approach, style, or intent), include the user's own key phrases in the memory content.
Do not replace the explicit creative-process description with a generic summary of emotions or motivations; capture both the stated feelings and the stated creative approach.
Stop after recording the explicitly stated description; do not infer additional techniques, add unmentioned details, or expand the memory further.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction often summarizes a user's artistic creation into a generic emotional summary and drops the user's explicit phrase describing the creative process, making later process-focused questions unanswerable. This skill ensures explicit descriptions of how a work was made are kept.

payload.name: Extract explicit first-person experience events
payload.description: Use during extraction when a speaker explicitly states an activity or experience they did, tried, or participated in, including in casual or photo-sharing messages.
content: During extraction, when a speaker explicitly states a concrete activity or experience they performed (e.g., 'I tried a new pose', 'we were trying out different poses', 'I read a book'), create an event memory capturing the speaker, action, object, and resolved time from the message timestamp.
Do not skip the candidate because the message also contains photos, feelings, or unrelated topics; extract each explicitly stated event separately.
Use the speaker's own words for named items; stop after capturing the stated facts and do not infer unmentioned details.

candidates.solves: Construction misses explicit first-person statements of activities or experiences when they appear in casual conversation or alongside photo-sharing, leaving later questions about those experiences unanswerable. This skill ensures concrete stated experiences are extracted as event memories.

payload.name: Preserve Explicit Companions in Event Memories
payload.description: When extracting an event or trip during which the speaker explicitly states they were accompanied by someone, include that companion as a participant in the memory content.
content: During extraction, if a message describes a trip, activity, or event and explicitly names a companion (e.g., 'my partner and I', 'with my friend'), include that person in the event memory content as a participant, not just the speaker.
Do not add companions unless they are explicitly stated; do not infer unmentioned people from context.
Stop after preserving the explicitly stated participants and the event's core details; do not add extra attributes or create separate memories per participant.

candidates.solves: Event extraction sometimes drops explicitly stated companions, so later questions asking 'with whom' or about joint activities cannot be answered. This skill ensures event and trip memories preserve all explicitly named participants alongside the speaker.

payload.name: Capture Emotional Reactions with Their Triggering Events
payload.description: Use during extraction when a message explicitly states a feeling or emotion about a specific event, feedback, or experience, even if the same message also contains plans, goals, or other facts.
content: During extraction, when a speaker explicitly states an emotional reaction (e.g., thrilled, rewarding, proud, excited) to a specific event, feedback, or achievement, create a memory candidate that captures both the triggering event and the stated feeling using the speaker's concrete wording.
If the same message also contains plans or goals, do not let them replace the reaction; preserve the emotional event as its own facet or memory and capture the plan/goal separately.
Stop after capturing the explicitly stated reaction and its trigger; do not infer unstated feelings or add details beyond the message.

candidates.solves: During extraction, when a message describes an event and also contains the speaker's emotional reaction to it, the reaction and its trigger are often omitted if the message includes other plans or goals. This leaves memory unable to answer questions about how the person felt or why, even though the evidence was explicitly present.

payload.name: Preserve Explicit Support Actions
payload.description: When a user states how someone supported or helped them with an activity or hobby, include the concrete action in the extracted memory instead of a generic support label.
content: During extraction, if a user explicitly describes how another person supported or helped them with an activity or hobby, capture the specific supportive action in the memory content; do not replace it with a generic label like 'support' or 'encouragement'.

Include the activity, the person, and the stated action (e.g., 'came to classes with me', 'played games with me', 'helped me study'), choosing the appropriate memory kind (event, relationship, or profile).
When later messages add or clarify the support action, UPDATE or MERGE the existing memory rather than creating a duplicate.
Stop after recording the stated action; do not infer or add supportive details not present in the message.

candidates.solves: When extracting memories from messages where a user explicitly describes a supportive or helping action (e.g., attending classes with them, playing games with them, helping them study), the extraction sometimes abstracts the action into a generic 'support' or 'encouragement' label, losing the specific detail needed to answer later questions about how the support occurred. This skill ensures the concrete action is preserved in the memory.

payload.name: Extract Separate Events from Speech-Act Messages
payload.description: When a message combines encouragement, advice, or reassurance with a speaker's own factual statement about an activity or experience, use this guidance to avoid omitting the event.
content: During extraction, when a message contains a speech act such as encouragement, advice, or reassurance, also identify any separate factual statements about the speaker's own activities or experiences and create distinct event candidates for them.
Treat a speaker's own past or ongoing event mentioned as support for a speech act (e.g., 'Last Friday at dance class...') as a separate event memory, not as detail of the speech act.
Before merging a candidate into an existing memory, check whether it represents a different fact or event; if so, keep it as its own memory rather than merging it into a speech-act summary.
Stop after each explicit fact is captured; do not infer unmentioned details.

candidates.solves: Prevents omission of a speaker's own factual events when they appear in messages primarily containing encouragement, advice, or reassurance. Ensures distinct personal activities are extracted as separate event memories, and that merges do not bury them in a speech-act summary.

payload.name: Extract Reasons Behind Stated Choices
payload.description: Use when a user explains why they chose or decided on something, stating the reasons or considerations behind the choice.
content: During extraction, if a message explicitly states why the user made a choice or decision (e.g., 'I chose X because...', 'I wanted Y'), capture those reasons as part of the candidate memory instead of recording only the outcome or a vague summary.
Preserve each stated reason separately (e.g., personal style, customer comfort) rather than merging them into one generic descriptor.
When enriching or updating an existing memory about the choice, ADD the newly stated reasons to the memory content rather than overwriting previous facets.
Stop after capturing the explicitly stated reasons; do not infer unmentioned motivations.

candidates.solves: Conversations where a user explicitly states the reasons or considerations behind a choice or decision, and memory extraction records only the outcome or a vague summary, losing the rationale needed to answer future 'why' questions.
